items.quote: put to the sword anyone who follows her
items.contrast: The followers are the stated targets of the sword command, rather than the woman who is brought out and later executed.
items.reason: The command explicitly applies “put to the sword” to anyone following the woman. Her later death creates a credible confusion, but she is not the grammatical object of that particular command.

items.quote: Have you been fair to Jerub-Baal and his family? Have you treated him as he deserves?
items.contrast: The referent of “him” is Jerub-Baal, not Abimelek.
items.reason: The immediately preceding clause names Jerub-Baal and his family, and the singular “him” refers back to Jerub-Baal. Abimelek is instead the person whom the audience made king.

items.quote: He told them what Micah had done for him, and said, “He has hired me and I am his priest.”
items.contrast: Micah acted for the young Levite, who is speaking, rather than for the people questioning him.
items.reason: The young Levite is the speaker, so “him” and “me” refer to him, while “them” denotes his questioners. The stem’s “does something” is avoidably generic and also obscures the passage’s past-tense report.

items.quote: You mistake the shadows of the mountains for men.
items.contrast: Zebul identifies the perceived figures as mountain shadows rather than the people Gaal claims to see.
items.reason: The question targets Zebul’s correction of Gaal’s first claim. Zebul explicitly contrasts shadows with men.

items.quote: Finally all the trees said to the thornbush, ‘Come and be our king.’
items.contrast: “Our” refers to the trees, not to the gods and humans mentioned as enjoying the vine’s wine.
items.reason: All the trees are the speakers asking the thornbush to become their king. The earlier reference to gods and humans does not define the requested kingship.
